offline-arcgis-map: During a DRDO traineeship, I built a Java desktop application using the ArcGIS Runtime SDK to work with maps offline.

The project introduced me to an important constraint in geospatial software: large map images need a more efficient representation than loading everything at once. Tile packages made it possible to work with the map in pieces.
The application brought together map display, multiple tile packages, shapefile feature layers and coordinate inspection. A user could inspect features and view location details in different formats.
The archive includes the original map and feature-layer screenshots. The practical story is about adapting a platform’s capabilities to a focused offline workflow.
number-plate-recognition: This MATLAB project explored a sequence of image-processing steps for extracting a vehicle’s number plate and recognizing its characters.

The pipeline converted an input image to grayscale, applied morphological processing, used edge information to isolate a region of interest and converted that region to binary form. Individual characters were then segmented and matched against templates.

The project assumed a stationary vehicle photographed at a fixed distance. That constraint matters: the archive demonstrates a pipeline under those conditions, not an unrestricted real-world recognition system.
The original images show the input, intermediate processing and final output. A step-through presentation can make each transformation easier to follow.
search-algorithms: I explored inverted indexes, Boyer–Moore and Rabin–Karp using long-form text as the input.

An inverted index organizes where terms occur so later searches can use that structure. Boyer–Moore uses information about a pattern to skip possible positions during matching. Rabin–Karp uses rolling hashes to help compare candidate substrings.
The project’s value is in making the different approaches visible: what each method prepares, how it searches and which work it avoids or repeats.
The archive contains the original diagrams and implementation notes. A small interactive example can help readers compare the approaches without having to read a large code listing first.
image-preprocessing: This project explored preprocessing steps intended to make images more useful for object detection. The original article describes dehazing, a color-palette workflow and a neural-network detection example.

A before-and-after presentation should show the actual source images, with captions explaining what changed. A detection output should be presented as an example result, rather than a substitute for an evaluation across a dataset.

The original article reports a 0.722 confidence score and approximately 7.2 seconds for one high-resolution example. Those values do not establish overall model accuracy or a general performance benchmark.
interactive-web-platform: This screenshot survives from my original web portfolio. It is part of the record of my early interface work, alongside more fully documented mapping, search and image-processing projects.
The repository does not contain a complete implementation article for this project, so the archive presents the artifact without inventing a problem statement, user base or measured result.
